name: Carbon180 (Giving Green, 2021)
summary: US policy advocacy for carbon removal. A re-implementation of Giving Green's 2021 estimate of what Carbon180's federal policy work from 2019 to 2021 (the 45Q carbon capture tax credit and direct air capture hubs) cost per tonne of CO₂ removed or kept out of the air.

sections.title: Carbon180's estimated CO₂e reductions relative to business as usual
From cost per tonne to tonnes per dollar
sections.explainer: charityevals' step after Giving Green's bottom line: Giving Green reports dollars per tonne; the site needs tonnes per dollar, and how much air pollution those tonnes cut. The tonnes are CO₂ captured at plants that keep running or pulled from the air, so almost none come from burning less fuel: they count for their heat deaths, discounted over the decades until they come (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

sections.title: Staff pay below market
sections.explainer: charityevals' step, not Giving Green's: with credit by share of resources on, staff's pay below what they could earn elsewhere counts as an in-kind contribution and gets its share of the outcome. Off by default.

rows.label: 2-year extension of 45Q: CO₂e reductions 2022–28 (million tonnes)
rows.explainer: The Energy Act (in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021) gave carbon capture projects until the end of 2025, not 2023, to start construction and qualify for the 45Q tax credit. Giving Green doubles 45Q's expected annual reduction for the two extra years; the same in all three of its cases. Giving Green doesn't source the annual figure behind the 98 million.

source.title: Giving Green, Carbon180 cost-effectiveness analysis
source.note: Energy Innovation's model of the Build Back Better Act, read off its chart

rows.explainer: A higher 45Q credit, proposed in the Build Back Better Act (2021). Giving Green reads the 45Q slice off Energy Innovation's moderate scenario and sums 2022–28; its pessimistic and optimistic cases shift the start of the reductions by two years either way.

rows.label: Direct air capture hubs: CO₂e reductions 2022–28 (million tonnes)
rows.explainer: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (2021) funds regional direct air capture hubs. Giving Green assumes capacity grows exponentially from today's to the proposed 2030 capacity, under four goals for that capacity. Carbon capture research and development in the same act is counted as having no effect before 2028.

rows.label: Change in probability of a bill passing with Carbon180's provisions
rows.explainer: Giving Green's pessimistic, realistic and optimistic cases (1%, 3%, 5%), informed by conversations with carbon removal experts: Carbon180 only has a small effect on whether a bill passes with carbon capture provisions, the same for bipartisan and progressive bills. The sheet also lists how many years Carbon180 moves policy forward (2, 4, 6; Summary!B24:D24), but no formula uses it.

rows.label: Expected value of Carbon180 (million tonnes CO₂e)
Cost per change in tonne of CO₂e
rows.explainer: Giving Green's bottom line, realistic case: about $0.66 a tonne ($3.47 pessimistic, $0.24 optimistic). Giving Green notes that it counts only short-term effects of Carbon180's work, so it may understate the impact.

rows.label: Change in CO₂e per dollar (tonnes per $)
Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar
rows.explainer: One over Giving Green's cost per tonne. How much air pollution these tonnes cut is the row below.

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fuel
rows.explainer: Our judgment. 45Q pays for CO₂ captured at industrial plants and power stations that keep running (much of it then used to pump more oil from old wells) and for CO₂ pulled from the air: none of it is fuel not burned, so none cuts the fine particles behind most of the deaths in the shared climate rate. The high end allows for capture units that scrub sulphur before capturing CO₂; capture's own energy use pushes the other way.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
rows.explainer: The row the site's climate conversion reads (docs/normalization.md 2.5): the air-pollution deaths each of these tonnes avoids, as a multiple of the world average behind the shared rate, 1.46 air-pollution deaths per 10,000 tonnes of CO₂ from fossil fuels (Rethink Priorities). The conversion values every tonne for its heat deaths (discounted over the decades until they come) and adds "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂"'s air-pollution part times this row, at once. Here it is the share of tonnes from burning less fuel, at the world-average smoke per tonne; at 0, the fuel doesn't matter.

rows.label: Staff pay as a share of program cost
rows.explainer: Default for research, technical assistance and policy work: mostly people. Our judgment; we haven't seen this charity's breakdown.

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable jobs elsewhere
rows.explainer: Policy staff and scientists could typically earn considerably more in law firms, consulting, lobbying or industry. Our judgment.

rows.label: Salary forgone by staff per dollar of cost (in-kind donation)
Share of the full cost paid in cash
rows.explainer: With credit by share of resources, staff's forgone pay counts as part of the cost, and staff get their share of the outcome. Off, this is 100%.

rows.label: Tonnes of CO₂e averted per dollar donated
rows.explainer: The tonnes per dollar above; with credit by share of resources, times the share of the full cost paid in cash (staff's forgone pay is the rest). The site turns these tonnes into years of healthy life through the deaths they avoid: "Deaths caused by one more tonne of CO₂", its heat part discounted over "Years until the heat deaths from a tonne of CO₂" for every tonne, and its air-pollution part, at once, times "Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne" above.
